content.title: About
content.content: Alcoholic malt beverage, sweetened, is a low‑alcohol or non‑alcoholic drink produced by fermenting barley malt and adding sugar. It has a sweet taste, mild carbonation, and a characteristic malt aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Malt beverages have a long tradition in Northern Europe and North America.
Sweetening reduces the natural bitterness of malt, making the drink more appealing to a broad audience.
Some recipes use honey or molasses instead of plain sugar, giving a distinct flavor profile.
The drink is often served chilled in summer as a beer alternative.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Malt extract provides vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds formed during malt roasting have antioxidant properties.

items.title: May aid digestion
items.content: A small amount of natural enzymes can help with food digestion.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Even low alcohol levels may be unsuitable for children, pregnant women, and those abstaining from alcohol.

items.title: High sugar level
items.content: Sweetened versions contain considerable sugar, which can affect blood glucose.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Carbonation may cause discomfort for people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve chilled as a refreshing beverage. It can be used in cocktails, mixed with fruit juices, or paired with light snacks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dark place with the package tightly sealed. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Avocado (Persea americana) is a creamy, nutrient-rich fruit native to Mexico and Central America. It has green or dark, bumpy or smooth skin, a buttery pale-green flesh, and a large central seed. Unlike most fruits, avocados are high in healthy fats. They are eaten fresh in salads, spreads such as guacamole, sandwiches, and smoothies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically, an avocado is a large berry with a single seed.
Avocados ripen after they are picked, not while still on the tree.
The Hass variety is the most widely grown and has dark, pebbly skin when ripe.
Unlike most fruits, avocados contain mostly fat and little sugar.
Avocado has been cultivated in the Americas for thousands of years.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fat
items.content: Avocados contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Avocados are a good source of fiber, which supports normal digestion.

items.title: Contains potassium and folate
items.content: These nutrients support normal blood pressure and cell function.

items.title: Provides vitamins K, E, and C
items.content: These vitamins support blood clotting, act as antioxidants, and support the immune system.

items.title: Helps absorb fat-soluble nutrients
items.content: The fat in avocado may help the body absorb carotenoids and vitamins A, D, E, and K from other foods.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Avocados are calorie-dense, so portion size matters.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people with latex allergy may react to avocado, and oral allergy symptoms can occur.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Avocado contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts may cause bloating in people sensitive to certain fermentable carbohydrates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Avocado can be sliced on toast, added to salads, sandwiches, and bowls, mashed into guacamole, or blended into smoothies and desserts. It is usually eaten raw, since heating can make it taste bitter. Ripe avocado yields slightly to gentle pressure.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unripe avocados at room temperature until they soften slightly. Ripe avocados can be refrigerated for a few days to slow further ripening. Cut avocado can be sprinkled with lemon juice, wrapped tightly, and refrigerated for a day or two. Avocado pulp can also be frozen.

chicken-or-turkey-noodles-and-vegetables.title: Chicken or Turkey with Noodles and Vegetables (no carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy); Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender chicken or turkey meat, boiled noodles, and a mix of vegetables (such as bell pepper, zucchini, peas) served with a flavorful gravy. It provides protein, carbohydrates, and vitamins while excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are among the most widely consumed poultry meats worldwide.
Noodles, made from wheat or rice, appear in over 100 culinary traditions.
Vegetables like bell pepper and zucchini are rich in vitamin C and antioxidants.
Gravy is often prepared from broth, cream, or tomato base, giving the dish a rich taste.
The recipe can be easily adapted for dietary needs by swapping noodles for gluten‑free or vegetable alternatives.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbohydrates
items.content: Noodles supply quick‑release carbs that replenish muscle glycogen stores.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, and potassium, supporting immunity and heart function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Skinless poultry contains little saturated fat, making the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Gravy increases the liquid content of the meal, aiding nutrient absorption.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared sauces can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions or make gravy from scratch.

items.title: Cross‑contamination
items.content: Keep raw meat separate from ready‑to‑eat foods to prevent foodborne illness.

items.title: Gluten in noodles
items.content: Traditional wheat noodles contain gluten; people with celiac disease should use gluten‑free alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing noodles, chicken or turkey pieces, and vegetables, then drizzling with gravy. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) for extra aroma. Suitable as a main course for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee Latte Nonfat Flavored is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from espresso, nonfat milk, and natural flavorings. It combines the strength of coffee, the creamy texture of latte, and a light fruit or vanilla note while containing virtually no fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Latte comes from the Italian word “latte,” meaning “milk.”
Nonfat milk retains most of the protein and calcium but almost no fat.
Flavorings are often derived from natural extracts of berries, vanilla, or caramel.
Latte is frequently served in large glasses to highlight the balance between coffee and milk.
In many countries, low‑fat latte versions are popular among calorie‑conscious consumers.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee provides polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine in coffee enhances alertness and concentration.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Nonfat milk maintains a high calcium level important for bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The lack of fat makes the drink suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee contains vitamins B2 and B3, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis sufferers.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Certain flavorings may contain artificial sweeteners that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume the beverage cold or warmed, adding ice for hot weather. You can also sprinkle cinnamon or cocoa powder on top to enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, it is best consumed within 7‑10 days, or keep refrigerated for longer freshness.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg Omelet with Cheese, Meat and Dark‑Green Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: An omelet or scrambled eggs enriched with cheese, lean meat (such as ham or chicken) and dark‑green vegetables (spinach, broccoli, kale) is a nutrient‑dense dish rich in protein, B‑vitamins, vitamin K, iron and calcium. Prepared without added oil, it has a low fat content (NS).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable complete protein sources.
A modest amount of cheese enhances flavor and adds calcium.
Dark‑green vegetables provide lutein and zeaxanthin – antioxidants beneficial for eye health.
Meat boosts iron and vitamin B12, essential for blood formation.
The omelet can be easily adapted for dietary restrictions, including gluten‑free or vegetarian versions.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B2, B6 and B12 aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from cheese
items.content: Help maintain strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Antioxidants from green vegetables
items.content: Lutein, zeaxanthin and vitamin K protect vision and support blood clotting.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: When cooked without oil, the omelet remains light, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should limit yolk intake.

items.title: Sodium in cheese and meat
items.content: Excess salt can raise blood pressure; choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor salmonella; cook until fully set.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, garnish with fresh herbs, add avocado slices or tomatoes. It’s convenient for a lunch box and pairs well with whole‑grain bread or a vegetable salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a microwave or skillet without added oil.

content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal (regular or quick‑cooking) is made from whole oat flakes prepared with non‑dairy milk and contains no added fat. It is a nutritious breakfast low in saturated fat, rich in fiber and slow‑digesting carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 5,000 years.
Oat flakes come in whole, rolled, or instant varieties.
Cooking with plant‑based milk makes the dish suitable for vegans and lactose‑intolerant individuals.
Oats contain beta‑glucans, which help lower cholesterol levels.
Oatmeal is a staple in sports nutrition because of its high complex‑carb content.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain stable blood sugar.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucans
items.content: These soluble fibers can reduce LDL (bad) cholesterol.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats provide thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Oatmeal supplies magnesium, iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for bones, muscles, and immunity.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Prepared without added fats, it remains a light option for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are often processed on equipment that handles wheat, so they may contain gluten. Choose certified gluten‑free oats if you have celiac disease.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Oats contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in very large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook oatmeal on the stovetop, in the microwave, or with hot water, adding plant‑based milk (almond, soy, oat). Sweeten or flavor with fruit, berries, nuts, cinnamon, or vanilla as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry oat flakes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked oatmeal can be kept in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Ribs are cuts of meat taken from the pork chest or back area. In the NFS (National Food Standards) catalogue they are classified as ready‑to‑cook meat products. Ribs have a rich, savory flavor, juicy texture and are commonly used for barbecue, roasting and braising.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork ribs are often marinated in spice blends and sauces before cooking to enhance flavor.
In the United States, ribs are traditionally slow‑cooked in smokers, giving them a distinctive smoky taste.
Japanese "tebbe" ribs are glazed with a sweet‑salty teriyaki sauce and grilled.
There are several types of ribs: baby back, spare ribs, and belly (brisket) ribs.
When cooked properly, the meat becomes so tender that the bones easily separate.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ribs provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The iron in pork is readily absorbed and supports normal blood formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ribs are rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, which support the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: Rib meat contains collagen that turns into gelatin during slow cooking, beneficial for joints and skin.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Ribs can be fatty, so people with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens (Salmonella, E. coli). Cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to pork.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Prepared marinades often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ribs can be baked, grilled, smoked or braised. They are frequently marinated in a mixture of soy sauce, honey, garlic and spices. Serve with barbecue sauce, mustard or a spicy glaze. Cut into serving portions and eat with your hands.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh ribs should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Frozen ribs can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature. Discard any ribs with a sour smell or discoloration.
